<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception
</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">
<span id="id1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_parbox ltx_align_top" style="width:385.5pt;">
<span id="id1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left"><span id="id1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lai Wei, Yatai Li, Liangbo He,
Jun Lan, Renjie Gu, Linhan Cao, 
<br class="ltx_break">Junkai Lin, Huijia Zhu,
Weiqiang Wang, Linghe Kong, Yue Wang, 
<br class="ltx_break">Zhuosheng Zhang, Weiran Huang 
<br class="ltx_break"></span>School of Computer Science, Shanghai Jiao Tong University  Ant Group</span>
<span id="id1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_left">Zhongguancun Academy  Shanghai Innovation Institute  Fudan University</span>
</span>
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Multimodal perception forms the foundation of multimodal intelligence.
In particular, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding are two pivotal tasks that underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents. However, synthesizing targeted, high-quality training data for these tasks remains difficult and costly.
Our key insight is that these tasks share an underlying capability, which we call connecting evidence: identifying relevant visual facts, binding them to the correct entities, recovering their relations, and composing them into an answer.
Crucially, targeted training data are far easier to synthesize for this capability than for these tasks themselves.
To strengthen this capability, we propose <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">EvidenceConnect</span>, an easy-to-implement data synthesis framework that uses zoomed views of related regions within a single image to generate questions requiring comparison, aggregation, or chaining of visual evidence.
To ensure quality, a reference answer is retained only when independent VLMs agree on it, and region-ablation tests discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions.
We then train base VLMs on the resulting data with RLVR, obtaining Zooming without Zooming v2 (ZwZ2).
Although the synthesized data are not tailored to any downstream benchmark, ZwZ2 improves fine-grained and spatial perception, with further gains on embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning (shown in Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
These results establish <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">EvidenceConnect</span> as an effective framework for supervising evidence connection and suggest that strengthening this shared capability leads to more generalizable multimodal perception.</p>
  
</div>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Multimodal perception is the foundation of multimodal intelligence: before a multimodal model can reason or act, it must determine what is present in a scene. Recent progress on this front, such as multimodal Chain-of-Thought <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li and Ma, 2026</a>)</cite> and Thinking-with-Images <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025c</a>)</cite>, has improved the ability of open-source vision-language models (VLMs) to perceive fine-grained visual content and use it in reasoning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2026b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, these advances do not reliably extend to tasks in which critical visual cues are dispersed across objects, relationships, frames, or dialogue turns. Two such tasks, spatial perception and multimodal long-context understanding, are particularly important because they underpin embodied AI and multimodal agents, respectively.
Spatial perception requires a model to recover how entities are arranged relative to one another and how several spatial relations compose <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gemini Robotics Team, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>. Embodied AI relies on it to ground navigation, manipulation, and viewpoint-dependent decisions in object locations and spatial relations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brohan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>. Multimodal long-context understanding requires a model to locate evidence across images and dialogue history, preserve entity identity, and bring that evidence to bear on the current question <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025d</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Multimodal agents rely on it to retrieve relevant past observations, resolve references across interactions, and integrate earlier evidence into current decisions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">He et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Su et al., 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Strengthening these capabilities, however, is constrained by the difficulty of building high-quality training data.
For spatial perception, existing efforts mainly scale up region-grounded relational data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>, but reliable labels require precise localization and relational grounding across multiple objects. Such labels are expensive to annotate by hand, while automated generators often hallucinate relations.
For long-context understanding, existing multi-image and multi-turn instruction data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> concentrate on a few formats and task types, because diverse questions that remain answerable over long sequences are hard to construct automatically.
Data for embodied spatial reasoning and multimodal agents are even harder to synthesize, since they additionally involve physical or interactive environments and multi-step trajectories. Consequently, neither these capabilities nor the applications built on them have a scalable and high-quality source of clean, verifiable supervision.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Our key insight is that these tasks build on a shared atomic capability of VLMs, which we call <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">connecting evidence</em>: identifying task-relevant visual facts, binding each fact to the correct entity, recovering the relations among them, and integrating the evidence into an answer.
These tasks instantiate this capability differently: spatial perception connects objects within a scene through spatial relations, whereas long-context understanding, on which multimodal agents rely, connects facts across images and dialogue turns through entity identity and reference.
Despite these differences in where the evidence resides and how it is linked, both tasks rely on the same underlying steps, so strengthening these steps can benefit both. Moreover, since the first step, identifying visual facts, is itself fine-grained perception, fine-grained perception benefits as well.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Crucially, training data that target this capability are far easier to construct and verify than data for the tasks themselves. To turn this insight into trainable supervision, we propose <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">EvidenceConnect</span>, an easy-to-implement, fully automated framework that synthesizes visual questions requiring the model to connect evidence across regions.
Specifically, we select a group of related regions within a single image and synthesize a compositional question over them from <em id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">privileged</em> zoomed views, which make small details visible but are used only during data construction.
Depending on the scene, we synthesize questions to compare, aggregate, or chain evidence across the regions.
Answering such questions thus exercises the same steps as the target tasks: relating regions spatially, including from a given viewpoint, parallels spatial perception and embodied spatial reasoning, whereas locating scattered regions, binding their facts to the right references, and integrating them parallels long-context understanding and multimodal agents.
To ensure data quality, we keep a question only if VLMs from different families agree on its answer, and we use region-ablation tests to discard questions whose answer survives the removal of selected regions.
Finally, each verified question is converted into multiple-choice form for rule-based rewards and paired with the full image, where colored outlines typically mark the selected regions to avoid ambiguous references, so the model must still perceive and connect the evidence by itself.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate whether this supervision generalizes beyond the synthesized questions, we train Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B, and Qwen3.6-27B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026b</a>)</cite> with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lambert et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI, 2025</a>)</cite> using only our synthesized data, without supervised fine-tuning or benchmark-specific question formats.
The resulting models, ZwZ2-4B/9B/27B, achieve substantial improvements in fine-grained and spatial perception as well as multimodal long-context understanding, with gains that further extend to embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning.
For example, ZwZ2-4B improves over its base model from 37.43 to 45.26 (+7.83) on ViewSpatial-Bench (spatial reasoning) and from 60.08 to 70.08 (+10.00) on MileBench (long-context understanding).
More broadly, its average over all 25 benchmarks increases from 49.41 to 54.79, and the corresponding averages improve from 51.63 to 56.59 for ZwZ2-9B and from 55.52 to 60.51 for ZwZ2-27B.
Notably, although ZwZ2 is trained only on single images, it also improves on multi-image long-context benchmarks and multimodal agent tasks. These results demonstrate that connecting evidence is indeed a generalizable training target for multimodal perception.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">To summarize, our key contributions are the following:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:0.5cm;">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We identify connecting evidence as an important atomic capability of VLMs, underlying fine-grained perception, spatial perception, and multimodal long-context understanding.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We develop <span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">EvidenceConnect</span>, a structured and audited synthesis pipeline for single-image, multi-region compositional questions, with privileged region views and independent checks for answer correctness and evidence dependence.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Experiments demonstrate that RLVR on the resulting synthetic data improves a broad range of perception benchmarks and further generalizes to many real-world tasks, including embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal agent tasks, and general visual reasoning.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Spatial perception.</span>  
Spatial perception underpins embodied tasks such as robotic manipulation and embodied question answering <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brohan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gemini Robotics Team, 2025</a>)</cite>.
Existing approaches use large-scale spatial supervision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, intermediate visual grounding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>, and progressive training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>.
Benchmarks and associated training resources examine perspective-taking, multi-image inference, and multi-hop composition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
MultihopSpatial additionally studies grounded spatial training and its transfer to embodied tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Euclid’s Gift <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lian et al., 2026</a>)</cite> demonstrates transfer from geometric surrogate tasks.
Similarly, we train on a surrogate task and evaluate its transfer, but our task is built from natural images and targets the evidence connection shared by spatial perception and long-context understanding, rather than spatial skills alone.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Long-context multimodal understanding.</span>  
Multimodal long-context understanding requires locating, tracking, and integrating evidence across long sequences of images and dialogue turns.
Existing efforts support these abilities through multi-image and multi-turn instruction tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and dialogue-fragment retrieval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bi et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, while benchmarks assess long-context integration and memory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025d</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
Controlled studies nevertheless identify persistent difficulties in aggregating distributed visual information <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Das et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
We target evidence connection as a shared component of these tasks, constructing single-image questions that require identifying, binding, and composing facts across regions.
This setting makes the selected evidence easier to localize and audit, allowing us to investigate whether such supervision transfers to multimodal long-context understanding without training on long image sequences or dialogue histories.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multimodal synthetic data.</span>  
Early resources provide annotated scene graphs and programmatic questions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krishna et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hudson and Manning, 2019</a>)</cite>. Later methods automate instruction generation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>, evolution <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, and synthesis for unsupervised post-training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>.
Zooming without Zooming <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2026</a>)</cite> transfers single-region supervision to full images with cross-model answer checks.
CRIT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sung et al., 2026</a>)</cite> and FM2DS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abaskohi et al., 2024</a>)</cite> synthesize cross-modal questions and filter unimodal shortcuts, while MM-CondChain <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shen et al., 2026</a>)</cite> verifies conditional programs and ReasonVQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tran et al., 2025</a>)</cite> composes external knowledge paths.
HopChain <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2026</a>)</cite> targets long-CoT robustness through instance-dependent chains with human-verified answers.
Unlike these pipelines, <span id="S2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">EvidenceConnect</span> builds each question on a coherent group of regions rather than a single region or a sequential chain, so its questions cover aggregation and closed-set comparison in addition to dependency chains.
Moreover, it automatically checks both the answer and its dependence on the selected regions, through cross-model agreement and region ablation, without human annotation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Boosting Multimodal Perception by Learning to Connect Visual Evidence</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As discussed in Section <a href="#S1" title="1 Introduction ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, fine-grained perception, spatial perception, and multimodal long-context understanding share a core capability that we call connecting evidence.
This motivates training data whose questions structurally require this capability and end in concise answers suitable for verifiable rewards.
To construct this supervision, we propose <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">EvidenceConnect</span>, a data synthesis framework centered on coherent groups of image regions. Within this framework, high-resolution privileged crops render local details visible for question synthesis, while cross-model answer anchoring and region ablation check label reliability and evidence dependence.
The overview of the data synthesis pipeline is shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Boosting Multimodal Perception by Learning to Connect Visual Evidence ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2610.37037v1/method.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:543/238;" width="543" height="238" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Overview of our multi-region question synthesis pipeline. We select related regions from a single image and construct a privileged crop view to generate compositional questions. The illustrative example connects a flight number on a boarding pass to its departure gate and then to a service icon (T218 <math id="S3.F2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> C6 <math id="S3.F2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> plug). Cross-model answer anchoring and drop-one region tests assess answer reliability and evidence dependence, followed by multiple-choice conversion and difficulty filtering. During training, the policy receives the full image with region outlines, while privileged crops are used only for data construction.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Multi-region Question Synthesis</h3>

<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Target question structure.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first define the target question, whose answer depends on connecting one coherent group of regions in an image.
Formally, from a source image <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="I" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>I</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">I</annotation></semantics></math>, we obtain localized region proposals <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{I}</annotation></semantics></math> and select one evidence group
<math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="G=\{r_{i_{1}},\ldots,r_{i_{k}}\}\subseteq R_{I},3\leq k\leq 7." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mo>⊆</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>I</mi></msub></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>≤</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>≤</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">G=\{r_{i_{1}},\ldots,r_{i_{k}}\}\subseteq R_{I},3\leq k\leq 7.</annotation></semantics></math>
Restricting the evidence to a single image keeps training inexpensive, while several related regions of one image already require a model to locate, bind, and compose dispersed evidence.
Importantly, the regions are selected to jointly support one question <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math>, which assigns each of them a role, i.e., the fact it contributes: a value to be combined, a member of a closed candidate set, or a clue on which a later step depends.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Corresponding to these three kinds of roles, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> connects the regions through one of three forms.
<em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Aggregation</em> combines counts or other numeric facts from the regions, possibly through a short calculation.
<em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Comparison and matching</em> treats the regions as the complete candidate set, so that an answer such as an outlier, an extremum, or a pairing can be identified only by considering all of them.
<em id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Dependency chains and compositions</em> build the answer in several steps, e.g., by using a clue to decide what to read next, fixing a viewpoint for interpreting the rest, or combining predicates from different regions.
In all three forms, the answer is determined only when the assigned roles are taken together.
These forms also tie our questions to the target tasks: spatial relations, including those in an agent’s or object’s own frame, parallel spatial perception and embodied spatial reasoning, while binding facts to regions referenced by outline colors and integrating them parallels how long-context understanding and multimodal agents handle facts tied to image or turn references.
To synthesize such questions, we first locate candidate regions, then group those that support one of the three forms, and finally compose questions over each selected group.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Grounded evidence discovery.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since multi-region questions need detail-rich scenes, we start from high-resolution, visually complex images.
For each image, a strong VLM judges whether it can support such questions and, if so, is prompted to propose concrete, clearly localizable regions, each with a bounding box and a short description, prioritizing regions that can be related to one another over isolated salient ones.
We then discard proposals that are too small, too large, or heavily overlapping.
As these model-generated descriptions may be wrong, they only guide grouping and question writing, whereas reference answers are later derived from the image itself.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Task-conditioned evidence grouping.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An arbitrary collection of these proposals, however, does not necessarily support a valid compositional question.
We therefore prompt a strong model with the image caption and region descriptions to propose several groups per image, each labeled with a task family (a specific question type such as anomaly detection) and a necessity mode (how removing a region should affect the answer).
We then discard invalid or duplicated groups and closed sets of incomparable objects, and keep groups with distinct task families first.
The task family only guides question writing, whereas each region’s concrete role is fixed when a question is written.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Privileged evidence layout.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since fine-grained details are difficult to inspect at full-image scale, we construct for each group a privileged evidence layout <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>G</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{G}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is accessible only during data construction.
Following the layout-preserving design of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2025)</a></cite>, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>G</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{G}</annotation></semantics></math> arranges native-resolution crops of the selected regions, with small context margins, on a compact canvas that removes irrelevant background while preserving their relative horizontal and vertical order.
In addition, each region is outlined in a distinct color that also marks it in the full image, allowing questions to refer to regions by color unambiguously.
Finally, <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>G</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{G}</annotation></semantics></math> serves as the sole visual input to the question generator, which confines its questions to evidence within the group, and it is later reused for verification (Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Two-stage Verification ‣ 3 Boosting Multimodal Perception by Learning to Connect Visual Evidence ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Question realization.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The question generator, a strong VLM, then receives <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>G</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{G}</annotation></semantics></math>, the region descriptions, and a few reasoning blueprints, i.e., templates of reasoning programs, and composes several candidate questions, each with a concise answer: a single value (e.g., a number, a short phrase, or the outline color of a selected region), a set, or an ordered pair.
To make its use of evidence checkable, the generator also states each region’s contribution and the answer expected after removing it, together with a reasoning certificate, i.e., a short sequence of steps that links the regions to the answer.
Deterministic rules then reject candidates whose certificate leaves a region unused or contains steps that do not lead to the answer, whose own predicted answer survives the removal of a region, or that use subjective wording, leak the answer through an outline color, or contain inconsistent arithmetic.
Implementation details and prompt templates appear in Appendices <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> and <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Prompt Templates for EvidenceConnect ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Two-stage Verification</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The checks above concern only the form of a candidate.
A compositional question, however, is useful supervision only if its reference answer is reliable and the intended evidence matters.
We assess these properties separately, since a plausible reasoning structure establishes neither.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Cross-model answer anchoring.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To obtain a more reliable reference answer, two VLMs from different model families answer <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> from <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>G</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{G}</annotation></semantics></math> several times, without seeing the region descriptions or the proposed answer.
A candidate is kept only if a clear majority of each model’s responses supports the same answer and this answer becomes the reference <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Adaptive drop-one testing.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Agreement on <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>, however, does not show that the answer actually depends on the selected evidence.
Since every question is constructed to require all of its regions (Section <a href="#S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" title="Target question structure. ‣ 3.1 Multi-region Question Synthesis ‣ 3 Boosting Multimodal Perception by Learning to Connect Visual Evidence ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>), an answer that survives the removal of a region indicates a defect, such as a decorative region or a shortcut that bypasses the intended reasoning.
To detect such defects, we mask each <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{i}\in G" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi>G</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{i}\in G</annotation></semantics></math> in the privileged layout, <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{G}^{-i}=\mathcal{M}_{i}(V_{G})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{G}^{-i}=\mathcal{M}_{i}(V_{G})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> replaces the crop of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> with a gray placeholder.
A verifier from one anchoring family then answers <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> from this view, reporting insufficient information if the masked evidence is needed, and either such a report or a changed answer confirms that the question depends on <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.
If instead <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> is still returned, or the response is unusable, we query the verifier again and mark <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> as <em id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">empirically redundant</em> only if most queries recover <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Note that a single redundant region, however, may reflect noise rather than a defect, because part of a masked region can remain visible in an adjacent crop through overlapping context margins, and individual responses also vary.
We therefore reject a question only when more than one region is redundant, which also improves synthesis efficiency, since a stricter rule would discard many potentially valid questions merely because one region was judged redundant.
The implementation details are shown in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Data Finalization</h3>

<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">From privileged crops to the policy view.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since the policy, i.e., the model under training, never sees <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>G</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{G}</annotation></semantics></math>, each verified candidate is paired with a policy view <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{I}</annotation></semantics></math>, by default the source image with each selected region outlined in its assigned color.
To avoid ambiguous references in the full image, these outlines mark which instances a question refers to, without revealing the answer-bearing content that the policy must still perceive and compose.
For aggregate questions, whose answers do not depend on the outlines, we also try to replace marker references with natural descriptions, so that the policy must locate the evidence itself.
This unmarked version replaces the marked one only if independent audits by both anchoring families, without access to <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>, confirm unique references, an unchanged multi-region task grounded in the intended regions, and the answer <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Multiple-choice conversion and difficulty filtering.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To support rule-based rewards in RLVR, we then turn each question into a four-option multiple-choice question, adding three distractors in the answer format of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> so that the format does not reveal the answer.
Each released example is thus <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x=(V_{I},\,q_{\mathrm{rel}},\,O)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>rel</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x=(V_{I},\,q_{\mathrm{rel}},\,O)</annotation></semantics></math> with label <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y\in\{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B},\mathrm{C},\mathrm{D}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>B</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y\in\{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B},\mathrm{C},\mathrm{D}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{\mathrm{rel}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>rel</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{\mathrm{rel}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the verified question stem, rewritten without marker references when the unmarked view is used, <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>O</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O</annotation></semantics></math> the shuffled option set, and <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y</annotation></semantics></math> the option of <math id="S3.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>a</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Finally, since overly easy examples provide little learning signal, a lightweight VLM answers each example several times, and we discard examples that it always answers correctly.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section evaluates whether learning to connect evidence within a single image yields improvements that generalize across multimodal perception tasks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">

<td id="S4.T1.2.34.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.8pt;padding-right:4.8pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.34.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EDDBED;">55.52</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.34.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.8pt;padding-right:4.8pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.34.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EDDBED;">54.79</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.34.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.8pt;padding-right:4.8pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.34.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EDDBED;">56.59</span></td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.34.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t" style="padding-left:4.8pt;padding-right:4.8pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.34.7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#EDDBED;">60.51</span></td>

</tbody>
</table></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">

<sup id="S4.T1.3.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S4.T1.3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">∗</span></sup>: extracted MMLongBench visual-core subset, including V-RAG,
Image MM-NIAH, and VH-Multi (25 non-Counting tasks in total).</p></div></div>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Settings</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Benchmarks.</span>  
We evaluate on 25 benchmarks in six domains (Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
<em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">(i) Fine-grained perception:</em> VStar <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu and Xie, 2024</a>)</cite>, HR-Bench 4K/8K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025c</a>)</cite>, MME-RealWorld (EN/CN) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025d</a>)</cite>, ZoomBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, Chartography <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Garre et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and PerceptionBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
<em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">(ii) Spatial perception:</em> TreeBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, O3-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2026c</a>)</cite>, CountQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tamarapalli et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, MIMIC <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Das et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, MMSI-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and SPAR-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>.
<em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">(iii) Multimodal long-context understanding:</em> MMLongBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025d</a>)</cite>, MileBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, and MemLens <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
<em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">(iv) Embodied spatial reasoning:</em> ERQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gemini Robotics Team, 2025</a>)</cite>, ViewSpatial-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025a</a>)</cite>, and MindCube-Tiny <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>.
<em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">(v) Multimodal agents:</em> AgentVista <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Su et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, together with ScreenSpot-Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> and UI-Vision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nayak et al., 2025</a>)</cite> for GUI grounding.
<em id="S4.SS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">(vi) General visual reasoning:</em> MMStar <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024b</a>)</cite> and BabyVision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2026</a>)</cite>.
We report accuracy (%) on all benchmarks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Training.</span>  
We train Qwen3.5-4B/9B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026a</a>)</cite> and Qwen3.6-27B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026b</a>)</cite> in non-thinking mode with GRPO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> on the 20.4K examples synthesized by <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">EvidenceConnect</span> (Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Training Data Statistics ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>), without supervised fine-tuning.
All three scales share the same data and training configuration (Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Training Details ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>), and we refer to the resulting models as ZwZ2-4B/9B/27B.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baselines.</span>  
We compare with two groups of baselines.
As references for absolute performance, Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> includes three advanced models: GPT-5.6-Luna, GLM-5.3-Flash, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.
To compare <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">EvidenceConnect</span> with existing synthetic training data, we further train Qwen3.5-4B with the same GRPO recipe on the datasets of ZwZ <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, TVG <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>, F<sup id="S4.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">2</span></sup>RVLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bi et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, CRIT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sung et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, and MMHops <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2026b</a>)</cite> (Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
For CRIT, whose 84,199 training samples contain 269,467 QA pairs from GQA, ActivityNet Captions, and SPIQA in multi-image, interleaved image–text, and multi-turn formats, we uniformly sample about 30K QA pairs across the three domains and train on them without CoT supervision or additional annotations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Main Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows that ZwZ2 improves over its base model on all 25 benchmarks at every scale, raising the overall average by 5.39, 4.96, and 4.99 points at 4B, 9B, and 27B, respectively.
In particular, fine-grained and spatial perception improve by 5.2–6.3 points on average, with gains of up to 11.1 points on MIMIC and 10.8 points on CountQA, and embodied spatial reasoning improves by 5.5–8.1 points, including 10.5 points on ERQA at 27B.
Qualitative examples are provided in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Case Study ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Notably, although ZwZ2 is trained only on single images, its gains carry over to multi-image and interactive settings.
Long-context understanding improves at every scale, most markedly at 4B, where the domain average rises by 5.6 points, including a gain of 10.0 points on MileBench.
Likewise, the multimodal agent benchmark AgentVista improves by 4.8–6.2 points, and GUI grounding also improves consistently.
These results support our premise that connecting evidence within an image transfers to tasks whose evidence spans images, dialogue turns, or interaction steps.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">ZwZ2 remains competitive with frontier models. ZwZ2-27B achieves the highest overall accuracy (60.51%), compared with 54.02%, 57.24%, and 55.47% for GPT-5.6-Luna, GLM-5.3-Flash, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, respectively, and leads the fine-grained perception domain.</p>
</div>

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Comparison with Existing Training Data</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> compares <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">EvidenceConnect</span> with existing synthetic datasets on the same 4B base model.
These datasets target single-region fine-grained perception (ZwZ), grounded counting and spatial reasoning (TVG), dialogue-fragment retrieval (F<sup id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">2</span></sup>RVLM), cross-modal multi-hop QA over interleaved contexts (CRIT), and knowledge-based multi-hop QA (MMHops).
Training on TVG, F<sup id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">2</span></sup>RVLM, CRIT, or MMHops improves MileBench but degrades HR-Bench, CountQA, MindCube-Tiny, and MemLens, and all four datasets lower the average accuracy below that of the base model.
In contrast, <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">EvidenceConnect</span> improves every benchmark over the base model and outperforms these four datasets on all 11 benchmarks, with a comparable amount of data (20.4K examples versus 19.4K–37K).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">ZwZ-73K is the strongest baseline.
Since it also synthesizes questions from zoomed-in views but grounds each question in a single region, the comparison with ZwZ serves as an approximate ablation of connecting multiple regions.
Although ZwZ uses 3.6<math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> as many examples (73K versus 20.4K), <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">EvidenceConnect</span> raises the average accuracy from 49.86 to 53.86 and surpasses ZwZ on 10 of the 11 benchmarks, trailing it only on MileBench by 0.13 points.
The largest margin appears on MindCube-Tiny, where ZwZ reduces accuracy by 13.8 points whereas <span id="S4.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">EvidenceConnect</span> improves it by 5.4 points.
This contrast is consistent with our premise that embodied spatial reasoning relies on connecting evidence across regions rather than on inspecting a single region.</p>
</div>
</section>

<td id="S4.T3.2.1.6.9" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.3pt;padding-right:1.3pt;">47.50</td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.6.10" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.3pt;padding-right:1.3pt;">45.68</td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.6.11" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.3pt;padding-right:1.3pt;">70.47</td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.6.12" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.3pt;padding-right:1.3pt;">42.14</td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.6.13" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6FFE6;padding-left:1.3pt;padding-right:1.3pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.6.13.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6FFE6;">52.65</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation study on drop-one verification.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate adaptive drop-one verification during data synthesis, we compare Qwen3.5-4B trained on 7K examples constructed with or without this verification step (Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).
As described in Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Two-stage Verification ‣ 3 Boosting Multimodal Perception by Learning to Connect Visual Evidence ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>, this step masks one selected region at a time in the privileged layout and tests whether the reference answer remains recoverable.
When the verifier returns the reference answer or an unusable response, additional queries are used; a region is marked as empirically redundant only if most queries recover the reference answer.
A question is rejected only when more than one region is empirically redundant, allowing for noise from overlapping crop margins and variable verifier responses.
With drop-one verification, average accuracy rises from 51.03 to 52.65 (+1.63 points), with improvements on 10 of the 11 benchmarks.
The largest gains are on MindCube-Tiny (+5.15), O3-Bench (+4.64), and CountQA (+3.79), while ERQA decreases by 4.00 points.
These results support the usefulness of this synthesis-time verification step for downstream performance, although its gains are not uniform across tasks.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablation study on privileged views.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To examine the role of privileged views, we train Qwen3.5-4B on 7K examples synthesized from privileged views or original images, with all other settings fixed (Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.4 Ablation Studies ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>).
Synthesis from privileged views achieves a higher average accuracy than synthesis from original images (52.65 versus 51.38), with higher scores on 9 of the 11 benchmarks.
Original-image synthesis performs better on Chartography and ERQA, by 4.00 and 4.75 points, respectively.
Thus, privileged-view synthesis improves average accuracy by 1.27 points in this 7K comparison, although its gains are not uniform across benchmarks.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Analysis</h3>

<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_align_left ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;position:relative; bottom:-185.0pt;"><span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:198.7pt;">
<span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_logical-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_top" style="width:96.4pt;">
                
<span id="S4.SS5.p1.p1" class="ltx_para"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.37037v1/qwen3_vl_before_after_vector.svg" id="S4.SS5.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:133/118;" width="133" height="118"></object>
</span>
                
<span id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<span class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Qwen3-VL generalization.</span>
</span>
              
</span>
<span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_logical-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_top" style="width:96.4pt;">
                
<span id="S4.SS5.p1.p2" class="ltx_para"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.37037v1/qwen35_4b_data_scale_vector.svg" id="S4.SS5.p1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:133/118;" width="133" height="118"></object>
</span>
                
<span id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<span class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Effect of training data scale.</span>
</span>
              
</span></span></span><span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Generalization to Qwen3-VL.</span>
To examine whether the gains extend beyond the base models used in the experiments, we evaluate Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B before and after training on the same 11 benchmarks in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.5 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports average scores of 36.82 and 41.63 for Qwen3-VL-2B, and 41.70 and 44.61 for Qwen3-VL-4B, corresponding to gains of 4.81 and 2.91 points, respectively.
These results suggest that the benefits of supervision extend to additional base models at both scales.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Effect of training data scale.</span>
Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.5 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> compares Qwen3.5-4B at different training data scales on the same 11 benchmarks.
Average accuracy over the 11 benchmarks in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> increases from 47.16 for the base model to 52.65 with 7K training examples and 53.86 with the full 20.4K training set.
The full set yields a further improvement of 1.21 points over 7K examples, while the 7K setting already improves over the base model by 5.49 points.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Context length.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Attention to evidence. ‣ 4.5 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> breaks down MemLens and the MMLongBench visual core by context length.
ZwZ2 outperforms or matches its base model at every length and scale, and on MemLens its gains persist up to 256K tokens.
The gains, however, narrow at the longest contexts.
At 128K on the MMLongBench visual core, for example, ZwZ2-4B and ZwZ2-9B merely match their base models.
This trend is consistent with our training data, in which each example contains a single image and thus a short context.
Training therefore strengthens evidence connection but not retrieval from very long inputs, which likely becomes the main difficulty at the longest lengths.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Attention to evidence.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To examine whether ZwZ2 focuses more on task-relevant visual evidence, we follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al. (2026)</a></cite> and evaluate ZwZ2-4B/9B against their base models on 405 TreeBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> examples equipped with annotated evidence bounding boxes.
For each full-attention layer, we compute the Intersection over Union (IoU) between the ground-truth evidence tokens <math id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>E</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E</annotation></semantics></math> and the <math id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|{}E|{}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|{}E|{}</annotation></semantics></math> visual tokens with the highest attention weights (Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Attention Map Coverage Analysis ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>).
As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Attention to evidence. ‣ 4.5 Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, ZwZ2 achieves a higher mean IoU across 7 out of 8 layers at the 4B scale and 6 out of 8 layers at the 9B scale.
This indicates that the high-attention tokens of ZwZ2 align more closely with the ground-truth evidence in most layers at both scales.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.fig3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:260.4pt;">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.37037v1/memlens_context.svg" id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:175/139;" width="175" height="139"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2610.37037v1/mmlongbench_context.svg" id="S4.SS5.SSS0.Px2.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:175/139;" width="175" height="139"></object></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Context-length performance on MemLens (left) and the MMLongBench visual core (right). </figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">

</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We presented <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">EvidenceConnect</span>, a fully automated framework that synthesizes multi-region visual questions and answers, requiring a model to connect evidence within an image.
Trained with RLVR on these data alone, ZwZ2 improves over its base models on all 25 benchmarks at 4B, 9B, and 27B.
Notably, although training uses only single images, the gains extend beyond fine-grained and spatial perception to embodied spatial reasoning, multimodal long-context understanding, and multimodal agent tasks.
These results suggest that connecting evidence is a transferable training target, and thus tasks whose training data are costly to build can benefit from data that are far easier to construct and verify.</p>
</div>
</section>

<div id="p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="p3.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Appendix
<br class="ltx_break" style="--ltx-break-space:14.2pt;"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Implementation Details</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section complements Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Boosting Multimodal Perception by Learning to Connect Visual Evidence ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> with the concrete settings used to construct our training data, following the order of that section.
The pipeline mainly uses Qwen3.5-397B-A17B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026a</a>)</cite>, and Table <a href="#A1.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Zooming without Zooming v2: From Seeing Details to Connecting Evidence for Generalizable Multimodal Perception" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> summarizes all model calls, each with the thinking mode disabled.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Model calls in the <span id="A1.T4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">EvidenceConnect</span> pipeline. <math id="A1.T4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{G}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>G</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{G}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the privileged layout, <math id="A1.T4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{G}^{-i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>G</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{G}^{-i}</annotation></semantics></math> the layout with region <math id="A1.T4.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> masked, and <math id="A1.T4.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{I}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{I}</annotation></semantics></math> the policy view.</figcaption>
